# Lakshmi Ganapathi on Consumer Stress & the Cracks Beneath the US Economy | The Real Eisman Playbook

First listed: 2026-02-09 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [YouTube: Lakshmi Ganapathi on Consumer Stress & the Cracks Beneath the US Economy | The Real Eisman Playbook](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jvfk3On7QnI) - 2026-02-09
- [Substack: Consumer VibeCession & Private Credit Risk with Lakshmi Ganapathi | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 45](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/consumer-vibecession-and-private) - 2026-02-09

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman tests Ganapathi’s consumer-stress and short-selling theses against stable bank data. She argues that BNPL, loan modifications and securitization conceal deteriorating affordability, then critiques FICO, Digital Realty and private credit. Eisman explains credit waterfalls and yen-carry risks and defends GE Vernova through concentrated gas-turbine supply and expanding power demand. Later company results support that operating thesis. Guest warnings about immediate data-center collapse and FICO displacement face contrary operating evidence, while uneven consumer credit data provide only partial confirmation of a second-half deterioration forecast.

Full transcript read. The strongest host operating thesis is GE Vernova gas equipment demand, supported by subsequent segment results. Guest collapse/displacement language outruns current operating evidence. Consumer stress is distributional and measurement-sensitive, so neither stable aggregate bank losses nor rising stock delinquency alone settles it.

<a id="Jvfk3On7QnI-c024"></a>
### 024. The yen carry trade earns a positive cross-currency interest spread if exchange rates are sufficiently stable, but yen appreciation can erase accumulated profits and leverage amplifies losses.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 26:30-28:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jvfk3On7QnI&t=1590s) | Stance: endorsed | Horizon: not stated

Assume unhedged yen funding, a higher-yield foreign asset, fixed borrowing terms and no defaults. Return in yen equals foreign asset return plus currency conversion change minus funding cost. Yen appreciation reduces the yen value of foreign assets while yen debt remains due; leverage multiplies equity sensitivity. A fully hedged trade also pays hedge costs.

Qualification: The 100-to-one example is illustrative, not a measured market leverage estimate.

Conditional reasoning: Assume unhedged yen funding, a higher-yield foreign asset, fixed borrowing terms and no defaults. Return in yen equals foreign asset return plus currency conversion change minus funding cost. Yen appreciation reduces the yen value of foreign assets while yen debt remains due; leverage multiplies equity sensitivity. A fully hedged trade also pays hedge costs.

Assessment test: Establish whether the stated yen carry mechanics proposition holds using matched primary disclosures; retain its conditions and separate causal explanations from price movements.

## Framework and tools

- Compare reported lender credit with borrower-level data and securitization pools.
- Map cash-flow cushions and refinancing dependencies before extrapolating equity outcomes.
- Separate a bad segment from the consolidated earnings driver; GE Vernova debate illustrates this.
- Avoid shorting cult stocks without a catalyst, according to the guest.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Bank charge-offs and provisions
- Consumer sentiment
- Auto and CRE ABS excess-spread waterfalls
- Loan modification and maturity data
- Yen funding versus foreign-asset yields
- Gas-turbine supplier concentration

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman hosts Lakshmi Ganapathi. Most bearish consumer, FICO and data-center propositions are hers. His questions, paraphrases and hypothetical arithmetic are distinguished from his asserted GE Vernova and credit-mechanics views.
- Opening montage repeats later discussion.
- Speaker transitions reconstructed from questions and answers; guest research claims are not automatically Eisman endorsements.
- GPI is confused with Genuine Parts in dialogue.
- Several numeric claims derive from anonymous sources, unspecified surveys or illustrative examples.
- No trade ledger or defined investment horizon for most shorts.
- New York Fed Q3 official indexed release inspected; direct page/PDF retrieval failed.
